title: The Priestly Garments and the Finished Work
summary: The craftsmen make the holy garments for Aaron and his sons: the ephod with its engraved shoulder stones, the breastpiece set with twelve gems for the twelve tribes, the blue robe hemmed with pomegranates and golden bells, the linen tunics and turbans, and the gold plate engraved HOLY TO THE LORD. The work is finished, the Israelites bring every part of the tabernacle to Moses, and Moses inspects it, sees that it was done as the LORD commanded, and blesses them.
story: This chapter brings the long construction account to its end. The garments described in chapter 28 are made, and then the entire tabernacle, piece by piece, is presented to Moses for inspection. The people who broke the covenant at the foot of the mountain have now done everything exactly as God commanded, and the chapter says so again and again. Moses' blessing at the end marks a moment of restoration. What remains is for the tabernacle to be set up and for God himself to fill it, which happens in chapter 40.
historical:
The high priest's garments reflect the splendor of royal and priestly dress in the ancient Near East, where fine linen, colored wool, and gold marked rank and sacred office. Egypt was renowned for fine linen, and gold thread made by hammering gold into thin sheets and cutting it into strips (verse 3) is a technique attested in ancient textiles. The ephod was a sacred vestment, apparently an apron or tunic-like garment; the word is also used for a simpler linen garment that the boy Samuel and King David wore (1 Samuel 2:18; 2 Samuel 6:14), and for an object Gideon made that became a snare to Israel (Judges 8:27).

The identity of the twelve stones is uncertain. The English names in translations are informed guesses based on the Hebrew words and the ancient Greek translation, and different versions render them differently. Ezekiel 28:13 describes the king of Tyre in Eden covered with precious stones, and nine of the stones in the Hebrew text match this list; the Septuagint's version of Ezekiel includes all twelve. Revelation 21:19-20 lists twelve jewels as the foundations of the new Jerusalem, several of which overlap with this list.
cultural:
The high priest represented the people before God and carried them with him when he entered the holy place. Their names were engraved on onyx stones on his shoulders as memorial stones (verse 7), and on twelve gems over his heart (verse 14), so that he bore them before the LORD both as a weight and in affection (28:12, 29). Seals engraved with names were a mark of identity and ownership in the ancient world, and the stones are engraved like a seal (verses 6 and 14).

The bells on the robe's hem let the sound of the priest's movements be heard as he ministered in the holy place, so that he would not die (28:35). The pomegranate, full of seeds, was a common symbol of fruitfulness and life, and it appears again on the pillars of Solomon's temple (1 Kings 7:18-20). The gold plate on the turban, inscribed HOLY TO THE LORD, set Aaron apart and, according to 28:38, allowed him to bear the guilt attached to Israel's holy gifts so that they would be accepted. The prophet Zechariah later pictures the same inscription on the bells of horses in Jerusalem (Zechariah 14:20), holiness spreading from the priest's forehead to the most ordinary objects.
literary: The refrain “just as the LORD had commanded Moses” marks the account of the garments seven times (verses 1, 5, 7, 21, 26, 29, 31) and returns three more times in the closing verses. The final verses echo the creation account in Genesis. In Hebrew, the work was completed (verse 32), as the heavens and the earth were completed (Genesis 2:1); Moses saw all the work (verse 43), as God looked upon all that he had made (Genesis 1:31); and Moses blessed them, as God blessed his creatures and the seventh day. The tabernacle is presented as a new creation, a small world ordered for God's dwelling. The Urim and Thummim, which were placed in the breastpiece according to 28:30, are not mentioned here, perhaps because they were not crafted by the artisans; Leviticus 8:8 mentions them again at Aaron's ordination.

outline.t: The ephod and its shoulder stones
The blue robe with pomegranates and bells
Tunics, turban, sash, and the holy gold plate
The finished work presented, inspected, and blessed

doctrines.note: The garments are called holy, and the gold plate declares the priest holy to the LORD. Holiness is conferred by God's command and marked visibly. The high priest is not holy by his own merit but by the office and garments God appoints.

The closing verses deliberately echo Genesis 1 and 2: work completed, seen, and blessed. The tabernacle is a small replica of the ordered world, and building it is presented as a renewal of God's purpose in creation to dwell with human beings.

The high priest carried the names of all twelve tribes on his shoulders and over his heart whenever he came before the LORD. Intercession here is not only words but a person bearing others before God.

words.note: Choshen, breastpiece, called in chapter 28 the breastpiece of judgment because it held the Urim and Thummim, the means by which God's decision was sought. It was a square pouch of woven fabric set with twelve stones, one for each tribe, and worn over the heart.

Zikkaron, memorial or reminder. The shoulder stones are memorial stones, so that God will remember the tribes when the priest comes before him. Remembering in the Old Testament is not merely recalling but acting on behalf of someone.

Tsits, literally a flower or blossom, used here for the shining gold plate on the front of the turban. Verse 30 also calls it the holy crown. Its inscription, HOLY TO THE LORD, was the high priest's most visible mark.

Barak, to bless. Moses blesses the people after inspecting the finished work (verse 43), echoing God's blessing on creation in Genesis 1. To bless is to speak favor and fruitfulness over someone, often with the authority of God.

christ: Hebrews presents Jesus as the great high priest to whom this office pointed: “Therefore, since we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold firmly to what we profess” (Hebrews 4:14). As Aaron carried Israel's names over his heart, Christ bears his people before the Father and always lives to intercede for them (Hebrews 7:25). Where Aaron needed a gold plate to declare him holy, Hebrews calls Christ holy, innocent, and undefiled (Hebrews 7:26). In Revelation, John sees the risen Christ “dressed in a long robe, with a golden sash around His chest” (Revelation 1:13), a description that recalls priestly as well as royal dress. The twelve jewels of the breastpiece reappear in the foundations of the new Jerusalem (Revelation 21:19-20), and the New Testament also calls believers a royal priesthood (1 Peter 2:9), sharing in the priestly calling Christ fulfills.
questions: The high priest carried the names of the tribes on his shoulders and over his heart. Whose names do you carry before God, and how?
The phrase just as the LORD had commanded runs through the whole chapter. Where is exact obedience hard for you, and why?
Zechariah imagined HOLY TO THE LORD written on horses' bells and cooking pots. What ordinary part of your life would look different if it bore that inscription?
